subsections.subsection_title: How to Report a NORMAL Respiratory Examination

blocks.text: “This is a [age]-year-old patient who is comfortable at rest and not in respiratory distress. There is no peripheral or central cyanosis, clubbing or peripheral edema. The respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute and the patient is not using accessory muscles of respiration.

The trachea is central and chest expansion is symmetrical bilaterally. Percussion is resonant throughout both lung fields. Breath sounds are vesicular with no added sounds. Vocal fremitus and vocal resonance are symmetrical. There is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

items: Overall, there are no significant abnormal respiratory findings.”

blocks.text: “The patient is comfortable and not in respiratory distress. Respiratory rate is 16 per minute. There is no cyanosis or clubbing. The trachea is central, chest expansion is symmetrical, percussion is resonant, and breath sounds are vesicular with no added sounds. Vocal resonance is symmetrical and there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.”

“There is reduced expansion of the right lower chest. Percussion is dull over the right lower zone. Breath sounds are bronchial with increased vocal resonance and vocal fremitus. There are associated coarse crackles. These findings are consistent with consolidation of the right lower lobe, in the appropriate clinical context.”

“There is reduced expansion of the right hemithorax. Percussion is stony dull over the right lower and mid zones, with reduced breath sounds, reduced vocal fremitus and reduced vocal resonance over the same area. The trachea is displaced to the left. These findings are consistent with a large right-sided pleural effusion.”

“There is reduced expansion of the right hemithorax. Percussion is hyperresonant on the right with markedly reduced breath sounds, vocal fremitus and vocal resonance. These findings are consistent with a right-sided pneumothorax.”
If trachea is deviated and patient unstable:

items: “The findings raise concern for a tension pneumothorax.”

blocks.text: “The patient has an increased anteroposterior chest diameter with reduced bilateral chest expansion. Percussion is hyperresonant and breath sounds are globally reduced with a prolonged expiratory phase and bilateral expiratory wheeze. These findings are suggestive of obstructive airways disease, particularly COPD in the appropriate clinical context.”

“The patient is tachypneic with increased work of breathing and bilateral expiratory polyphonic wheeze with a prolonged expiratory phase. There is reduced air entry bilaterally. These findings are consistent with an acute obstructive airway process such as asthma.”
“Given the marked respiratory distress and reduced air entry, this may represent a severe/life-threatening asthma exacerbation.”

“There is reduced bilateral chest expansion with fine, predominantly bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and associated digital clubbing. These findings suggest an interstitial lung disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis.”

“There is digital clubbing with bilateral coarse crackles, predominantly at the bases, with associated wheeze. The crackles partially change with coughing. These findings are suggestive of bronchiectasis.”

content_groups.group_title: Q: What is the normal respiratory rate?

blocks.text: 12–20 breaths/min in an adult at rest.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why count for a full minute?

blocks.text: To accurately assess rate and rhythm, especially if breathing is irregular.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What are signs of respiratory distress?

blocks.text: Tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal recession, nasal flaring, inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis and altered mental state.
Bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges associated with changes in the nail bed.

content_groups.group_title: Q: How do you test for clubbing?

blocks.text: Inspect the nails and perform Schamroth's window test.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What respiratory diseases cause clubbing?

blocks.text: Lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess and interstitial lung disease.
Clubbing is not a typical feature of uncomplicated COPD. If significant clubbing is present, consider another diagnosis such as lung cancer or bronchiectasis.

Q: What is normal lung percussion?

blocks.text: Consolidation, pleural effusion, collapse and mass.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What are normal breath sounds?

blocks.text: Loud, relatively high-pitched breathing with a prominent expiratory component and a possible pause between inspiration and expiration.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Where is bronchial breathing normally heard?
Q: When is bronchial breathing abnormal?

blocks.text: When heard over peripheral lung fields, particularly in consolidation.
Pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary edema are classic examples.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Do crackles clear with coughing?

blocks.text: Crackles due to secretions may change or clear with coughing; crackles from parenchymal disease typically persist.
A continuous musical sound caused by narrowed airways.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What is a monophonic wheeze?

blocks.text: A single-pitched wheeze, suggesting localized airway obstruction.
A harsh, predominantly inspiratory sound suggesting upper airway obstruction.

content_groups.group_title: Q: When is vocal resonance increased?

blocks.text: Pleural effusion, pneumothorax and severe emphysema.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why does consolidation increase vocal resonance?

blocks.text: Solidified lung transmits sound vibrations more efficiently than air-filled lung.
Dull + bronchial breathing + increased vocal resonance + increased fremitus.
Stony dull + reduced breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance + reduced fremitus.
Increased vocal resonance/fremitus and bronchial breathing may occur.
Usually reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance/fremitus.
Collapse tends to pull the trachea toward the affected side.
